name: Civil War, regicide, and the trial of the king
description: The literature of the English Revolution: the wars of the 1640s, the trial and execution of Charles I in 1649, and the contests over sovereignty, loyalty, and resistance that these events provoked, from Milton's republican defences of regicide and the Eikon Basilike controversy to the royalist elegies and the tracts of Hobbes and Harrington.

name: Liberty of conscience and religious toleration
description: The long argument over freedom of worship and belief that ran from the collapse of censorship in 1641 through the Restoration settlement and the Toleration Act of 1689, engaging Milton's Areopagitica, Locke's Letter Concerning Toleration, the Leveller petitions, the Cambridge Platonists, and the persecuted nonconformity of Bunyan.

name: Country retirement and the estate poem
description: The praise of rural retirement, the country house, and the landed estate as a moral and social ideal, from Denham's Cooper's Hill and the estate poems of Carew and Marvell ('Upon Appleton House') to Cowley's essays on retirement and the contrast between the corruption of the town and the virtue of the country.

name: Wit, libertinism, and the rake
description: The celebration and critique of libertinism, wit, and sensual freedom in Restoration culture — the rake-hero of the comedy of manners, the libertine verse of Rochester and Dorset, the hedonism of the court of Charles II, and the satirical and moral reactions against the age's sexual licence.

name: Restoration politics: party, succession, and Exclusion
description: The fierce partisan politics of the Restoration, above all the Exclusion Crisis (1679–1681) over the Catholic succession of the Duke of York, the birth of Whig and Tory, the Popish Plot, and the Revolution of 1688, which supplied the subjects of Dryden's Absalom and Achitophel and the political verse and prose of the age.

name: The New Science and experimental philosophy
description: The impact of Baconian empiricism, the Royal Society, and the new natural philosophy of Boyle, Hooke, Wilkins, and Glanvill on literature — the ideal of a plain, factual prose, the authority of observation and experiment, the critique of dogmatism, and the imaginative response in Cowley, Cavendish, and Milton.

name: Carpe diem and the pleasures of the present
description: The Horatian and libertine exhortation to seize the day and enjoy love, wine, and youth while time permits, from Herrick's 'Gather ye rosebuds' and the Cavalier songs to Marvell's 'To His Coy Mistress' and the Restoration lyrics, set against the period's equally strong sense of mutability and death.

name: Female authorship and the woman writer
description: The emergence of women as professional and published writers — Katherine Philips and Anne Finch in verse, Margaret Cavendish in philosophy and romance, Aphra Behn as the first professional woman playwright and novelist, and Mary Astell's feminist polemic — together with the literary and social debate over women's wit, learning, and place in print.

name: Slavery, empire, and the Atlantic world
description: The literature of colonial expansion, the Atlantic slave trade, and empire — Behn's Oroonoko and her Surinam setting, the discovery and plantation narratives, Dryden's and Davenant's Indian Queen, and the early critique of slavery and of the treatment of indigenous and African peoples.

name: Faith, grace, and the pilgrim's journey
description: The Puritan and Anglican literature of the soul's progress toward salvation — Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress and Holy War, Herbert's Temple, Traherne's Centuries, and the devotional prose of Taylor and the Latitudinarians — expressing the period's deep preoccupation with grace, election, and the Christian life as a pilgrimage.

name: The city and urban life
description: The representation of London and the town as the arena of wit, commerce, intrigue, and satire — the city comedies of Shirley and Brome, the coffee-house and playhouse society of Restoration comedy, Pepys's London, and the satirical anatomy of urban manners and corruption.

name: Reason, faith, and the limits of understanding
description: The philosophical inquiry into the powers and bounds of human reason and its relation to faith — Hobbes's materialism, Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding, the Cambridge Platonists' rational religion, Glanvill's scepticism, and Browne's Religio Medici — which defined the age's epistemology and prepared the Enlightenment.
